doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Tuning, variable and fixed pitch: erhu, yangqin and blues
summary: Combining Chinese and Western tuning, his experience playing Oakland blues joints, and how erhu inflection fits the blues.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did your combining of these certain elements, do you run into let’s say problem solving situations with scales that might be inherently Chinese and our music here, based on diatonic scales, etc. How do you work those together?

Well one of the questions I asked is the tuning, western and non-western tuning. And I kind of equate my experience when I used to perform in the joints — I didn’t perform in the blues clubs like in Oakland, and that was probably a learning lesson for me both in terms of music, and trying to respect the music, and also socially. Because it’s just very atypical for a Chinese-American to be performing in the joints in Oakland, in an African- American club. But when you have like a singer who is bending the pitch, the inflection, you have the variable pitch. You have a guitar that’s bending notes. The piano is a fixed pitch instrument but sometimes you have, you can create the illusion by clusters or grace notes and so forth. But that was never ever a problem, having variable pitched and fixed pitch instruments. Where in the Chinese orchestra you have like the erhu, which is a Chinese two stringed instrument which has that inflection bending that can fit right in in the blues. And you have other melodic variable pitch. But in the Chinese orchestra you also have the yanquin, which is a Chinese hammered dulcimer instrument. It’s trapezoidal shaped with metal strings across and it’s performed with a pair of bamboo sticks. And that’s similar to the piano which a hammer or stick is striking metal strings. And that’s a fixed pitch instrument. So it’s not like you have to think about like you have to be in tune. It creates this beautiful color. And just in a similar way when I listen to Miles Davis and Wayne Shorter, when they’re blending but sometimes there’s a beauty in that when things are not fitted perfectly.
But they are really fitted perfectly.
